claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.
A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.1 While loop

artifact.df: The test a while loop checks before each pass to decide whether to continue.
artifact.eg: In a password prompt, the condition can check whether the entry is still invalid.
artifact.mi: It is the code inside the loop body.
artifact.cx: The body does the work; the condition is the check that controls whether another iteration happens.

artifact.df: The event that causes a repeating sequence of code to cease execution.
artifact.eg: Setting a counter variable to a value that makes the loop condition false.
artifact.mi: Assuming the loop stops after the first time the condition is met.
artifact.cx: If the loop expression is false, the loop terminates.

claims: A dictionary stores key-value pairs and looks up each value by its key rather than by a numeric position.
Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.
Dictionaries are written with curly braces in key: value form and are ideal when data is naturally labeled rather than ordered.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §10.1 Dictionary basics

artifact.df: A label used to retrieve one stored value from a mapping.
artifact.eg: In a dictionary of course rooms, 'BIO101' can point to one room assignment.
artifact.mi: A key can repeat many times for the same mapping entry.
artifact.cx: Because lookup uses labels, the same key cannot be duplicated in one dictionary.

artifact.df: The constraint that every identifier used to access a stored item must be distinct.
artifact.eg: Ensuring that in a dictionary, no two entries share the same label.
artifact.mi: Assuming that the structure can accommodate multiple entries with the same label.
artifact.cx: Because a dictionary looks up values using keys, it cannot hold duplicate keys.

claims: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

artifact.q: A program needs the full text of a saved note file so it can count the characters. Which file method fits this task best after opening the file?
artifact.ex: read() is the best choice because it returns the entire contents as one string. A common misconception is to choose readlines(), but that produces a list of separate lines rather than one full string.

artifact.q: Which function retrieves the next single line from a file?
artifact.ex: read() returns the entire contents of a file and returns a single string. The misconception is using read() when only one line is needed; readlines() returns a list of every line.

claims: File I/O lets a program read information from and write information into files; a file is accessed by opening it, working with its contents, and closing it.
open() returns a file object that the program then reads from or writes to.
read() reads the entire contents of a file and returns a single string.
readline() returns the next single line, while readlines() returns a list with every line of the file.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §14.1 Reading from files

artifact.df: A way for a program to work with data stored in files by opening the file, using its contents, and then closing it.
artifact.eg: A student script opens a text file of survey answers, reads the lines, and then closes the file.
artifact.mi: It only means saving information, not reading it.
artifact.cx: It includes both reading from files and writing into files.

artifact.df: The data structure returned by the open() function that allows interaction with the file.
artifact.eg: Using the file object to call read() to get a string from the file.
artifact.mi: Thinking the file object is the file itself, rather than the handle to the file.
artifact.cx: The file object is the program's interface for reading or writing file contents.

claims: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.
The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

artifact.q: A lab group notes a rock layer that lies below the crust and above the core. Which Earth layer is this?
artifact.ex: The mantle fits because it is the layer below the crust and above the core. A common misconception is to choose the core because it is deeper, but the core is below the mantle, not between crust and core.

artifact.q: Which layer of Earth is described as solid rock that flows slowly due to convection?
artifact.ex: The asthenosphere is the correct choice because it is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat (Claim 3). The most plausible misconception is selecting the rocky mantle, which is described as thick and solid rock, not flowing.

claims: A volcano's eruptive style is set largely by magma viscosity, which rises with silica content: runny low-silica magma erupts gently, while sticky high-silica magma traps gas and erupts explosively.
Low-viscosity (low-silica, basaltic) magma flows easily like syrup, producing the gentle eruptions of Hawaiian shield volcanoes.
High-viscosity (high-silica, felsic) magma is thick and sticky and flows slowly like toothpaste, trapping gas until it erupts violently.
The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a fast cloud of hot ash and gas typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.4 Volcanic eruptions and hazards

artifact.q: A volcano is fed by magma that moves easily and produces gentle eruptions. Which magma type best fits that description?
artifact.ex: Low-silica magma has low viscosity, so it flows easily and tends to erupt gently. The tempting misconception is that any magma that erupts is sticky; in fact, the stickiest, most explosive magma is the high-silica kind.

artifact.q: What hazard is most characteristic of explosive high-silica volcanoes?
artifact.ex: The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a fast cloud of hot ash and gas typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes. (Misconception: Lava flow is the most dangerous hazard.)

claims: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.
The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.
The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.
The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

artifact.df: A mechanically weak upper-mantle zone that behaves like solid rock while moving slowly.
artifact.eg: Hot mantle material beneath a plate can circulate through the asthenosphere.
artifact.mi: It is liquid magma.
artifact.cx: It is solid rock that flows slowly by convection, not a liquid layer.

artifact.df: A distinct division of the planet's structure.
artifact.eg: The distinction between the crust, mantle, and core.
artifact.mi: Confusing the asthenosphere with the solid rocky mantle.
artifact.cx: The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat (Claim 3).

claims: Sedimentary rock forms when sediment is deposited, compacted under burial, and cemented into stone — a process called lithification — and its features record the depositional environment.
Compaction occurs as more material accumulates on top, squeezing the grains together.
Cementation glues the grains together with minerals; compaction and cementation together are lithification.
Clastic (detrital) sedimentary rocks are made of pieces of preexisting weathered rock.
The features of a sedimentary rock are read to reconstruct its original depositional environment.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §5.3 Sedimentary rocks

artifact.df: A sedimentary rock built from fragments of older weathered rock.
artifact.eg: Sandstone made from sand-sized bits eroded from preexisting rocks.
artifact.mi: It must form from dissolved minerals that crystallize directly from water.
artifact.cx: Clastic rocks are fragmental; they come from pieces of earlier rocks rather than direct chemical precipitation.

artifact.df: Sedimentary rocks made from pieces of pre-existing weathered rock.
artifact.eg: Shale or sandstone.
artifact.mi: Assuming all sedimentary rocks are clastic.
artifact.cx: Clastic rocks specifically consist of fragments of older rock.

claims: In music, a triad is a set of three notes (or "pitch classes") that can be stacked vertically in thirds.
A seventh chord is a chord consisting of a triad plus a note forming an interval of a seventh above the chord's root.
The seventh destabilized the triad, and allowed the composer to emphasize movement in a given direction.
There are four different inversions of a seventh chord.

artifact.df: A three-note sonority built by stacking notes in thirds.
artifact.eg: A student identifies C–E–G as a triad in a harmonic analysis.
artifact.mi: It must always contain four notes.
artifact.cx: A triad has three notes; adding a note a seventh above the root turns it into a seventh chord.

artifact.df: The vertical arrangement of notes that form a harmonic unit.
artifact.eg: A C major triad is C-E-G. A C dominant seventh chord adds a note to this structure.
artifact.mi: A chord is simply a collection of notes played simultaneously.
artifact.cx: A chord structure describes how notes are stacked vertically, which is the basis for understanding chord construction.

claims: In music theory, a scale is "any consecutive series of notes that form a progression between one note and its octave", typically by order of pitch or fundamental frequency.
A measure of the width of each scale step provides a method to classify scales.
Scales can be abstracted from performance or composition.
Therefore, any scale is distinguishable by its "step-pattern", or how its intervals interact with each other.
A specific scale is defined by its characteristic interval pattern and by a special note, known as its first degree (or tonic).
The expression scale degree refers to these numerical labels.

artifact.tr: The numerical labels used to name positions within a scale.
artifact.df: The scale degree refers to these numerical labels.
artifact.eg: In the C major scale, the first degree is C.
artifact.mi: Misconception: The scale degree is the name of the note itself.
artifact.cx: Correction: The scale degree is the numerical label assigned to that note's position in the scale.

artifact.df: A consecutive series of notes spanning one octave in order.
artifact.eg: C–D–E–F–G–A–B–C is a scale example.
artifact.mi: Any set of notes, even if unordered, counts as one.
artifact.cx: Order and octave span are required for the definition.

claims: In music, form refers to the structure of a musical composition or performance.
The term "binary form" is used to describe a musical piece with two sections that are about equal in length.
Musical form unfolds over time through the expansion and development of these ideas.
Form in music is the result of the interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].
Subdivisions of each large musical unit are shown by lowercase letters (a, b, and so on).
The next level concerns the entire structure of any single self-contained musical piece or movement.

artifact.df: A musical piece consisting of two sections of equal length.
artifact.eg: An A-B form where section A and section B are the same length.
artifact.mi: Binary form is the same as sectional evidence.
artifact.cx: The term 'binary form' is used to describe a musical piece with two sections that are about equal in length.

artifact.df: A pattern built from two sections that are about equal in length.
artifact.eg: A dance movement with an A section and a matching B section.
artifact.mi: It means any piece with exactly two notes or two measures.
artifact.cx: The label refers to two balanced sections, not to the number of notes or measures.

claims: In music, a triad is a set of three notes (or "pitch classes") that can be stacked vertically in thirds.
A seventh chord is a chord consisting of a triad plus a note forming an interval of a seventh above the chord's root.
The seventh destabilized the triad, and allowed the composer to emphasize movement in a given direction.
There are four different inversions of a seventh chord.

artifact.df: A chord formed by adding one note that creates a seventh above the root on top of a triad.
artifact.eg: In a tonal excerpt, a student marks a four-note sonority as a seventh chord because it includes a triad plus the seventh.
artifact.mi: It is just any chord with seven notes.
artifact.cx: The defining feature is a triad plus one note a seventh above the root, not the total number of notes.

artifact.df: A chord built upon a triad with an added note forming a seventh interval above the root.
artifact.eg: A seventh chord is formed by taking a triad and adding a note that creates a seventh above the root.
artifact.mi: A seventh chord is a chord consisting of only three notes.
artifact.cx: A seventh chord is defined as a triad plus a note forming a seventh above the chord's root.

claims: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

artifact.df: Turning user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
artifact.eg: Writing a user story like 'As a user, I want X so that Y'.
artifact.mi: This is simply stating a desired feature.
artifact.cx: This is need articulation, which translates high-level needs into actionable user stories.

artifact.df: A short feature-focused statement that expresses how a product should meet a user need.
artifact.eg: A team turns the need for fast access into a story about saving a draft from any device.
artifact.mi: It is the same thing as a raw user need.
artifact.cx: A need is higher-level and more stable, while the story describes features or content meant to address it.

claims: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

artifact.df: A higher-level requirement that tends to stay more stable than a single interface request.
artifact.eg: A participant’s need for fast, reliable task completion can be turned into several user stories for the prototype.
artifact.mi: A user need is the same thing as one exact button label or screen layout.
artifact.cx: The correction is that a need sits above individual interface requests and can lead to multiple stories.

artifact.df: A shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs.
artifact.eg: A profile representing a group of frequent commuters.
artifact.mi: A persona is just a collection of individual interface requests.
artifact.cx: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.

claims: Interactive prototyping builds a testable representation of how a planned experience looks and works without requiring every production detail.
Prototypes can be combined with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough to test whether a design concept works.
Functional prototypes allow a team to observe how users interact with a product.
A prototype should show the major interactions even when not every interaction is functional.
Prototypes should support fast iteration and be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them.

artifact.q: How can functional prototypes assist a team in understanding user engagement?
op: By showing only the major interactions.
By combining them with a cognitive walkthrough.
By allowing the team to observe how users interact with the product.
By requiring every interaction to be fully functional.
artifact.ex: The correct choice is functional prototypes allowing observation of user interaction. The misconception is that prototypes must only show major interactions, which is insufficient for observing interaction.

artifact.q: What is the main purpose of an interactive prototype in a UX lab when the final product is not yet built?
op: A testable model of how the experience looks and works without every production detail
A fully finished product that is ready for launch
A visual style guide that only shows colors and typography
A legal document that approves the design team
artifact.ex: The correct choice captures a testable representation that shows how the experience looks and works without requiring every production detail. The common misconception is that a prototype must be fully finished; in fact, it is meant to be learned from before production details are complete.

claims: A research-based persona is a shareable profile of a user group with similar behavior and needs, used to keep design choices connected to evidence.
Personas are one way to present research findings so other people can understand and share them.
User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
Teams turn user needs into user stories that describe features and content intended to meet those needs.
Keeping each user story linked to its source need enables evaluation of whether the need is being met.

artifact.df: A shareable profile built from research for one user group with similar behavior and needs.
artifact.eg: After interview synthesis, the team creates a persona for frequent mobile shoppers to guide prototype decisions.
artifact.mi: A persona is just a fictional mascot or decorative poster.
artifact.cx: The correction is that it summarizes researched patterns so the team can align choices with evidence.

artifact.df: High-level, stable requirements for a user group.
artifact.eg: The need for a mobile app to reliably send notifications.
artifact.mi: User needs are transient and change with every interface request.
artifact.cx: User needs are generally higher-level and more stable over time than individual interface requests.
